paras.text: Carpentry and Structural Framing — Michigan Builder Exam Audio Lecture

Alright, let's talk carpentry and framing. This is the single biggest trade category on the Michigan residential builder exam — sixteen of your one hundred ten trade questions come from here. Nothing else comes close. If you own this chapter, you've banked a seventh of the whole trade section. And here's the good news: almost every question in this domain is a number. A fraction of a joist depth, a percentage of a stud width, a nail count, an inch measurement. Numbers can be drilled, and that's exactly what we're going to do.

One framing fact before we start: the exam tests the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code. Not the twenty twenty one I R C. The newer code was stayed by a court order in July of twenty twenty five and never took effect. That matters because Michigan amended some values away from the I R C defaults, and the exam loves to dangle the national number as a wrong answer. Every time I flag something as a Michigan amendment, burn it in twice.

Let's start down at the floor. Every joist, beam, or girder needs bearing at its ends — one and a half inches minimum on wood or metal, three inches minimum on masonry or concrete. Say it with me: one and a half on wood, three on concrete. If a wood girder pockets into a concrete or block wall, it gets that three inches of bearing plus a half inch air space around the untreated wood so it doesn't rot.

Joist ends also need lateral restraint — full depth solid blocking at least two inch nominal, or attachment to a full depth header, band joist, rim joist, or an adjoining stud. That's the end of the joist. Now, mid span: here's a Michigan exam classic. Bridging — meaning solid blocking, diagonal bridging, or a one by three strip nailed across the bottoms — is only required for joists that exceed a nominal two by twelve, and when it's required, the intervals can't exceed eight feet. Hear the trap in that: a two by ten does not need bridging. A two by twelve does not need bridging. Only joists deeper than a two by twelve. The wrong answer on the exam will say two by ten. Don't take the bait.

Now cutting, drilling, and notching of sawn joists. This is pure fractions, and it shows up constantly. Notches in the top or bottom of a joist: maximum depth is one sixth of the joist depth, the notch can't be longer than one third of the depth, and no notches at all in the middle third of the span. At the very end of the joist, over a bearing, the notch can be deeper — up to one fourth of the depth. Holes are their own rule: maximum diameter one third of the depth, and every hole stays at least two inches away from the top edge, the bottom edge, any other hole, and any notch. So the pattern is: one sixth for notches in the span, one fourth for notches at the ends, one third for holes and for notch length, two inches of clearance everywhere. Run that on a two by ten, actual depth nine and a quarter: notch about an inch and a half, end notch about two and five sixteenths, hole about three and one sixteenth.

And engineered lumber? Different world. You do not cut, notch, or drill an I joist, an L V L, a glulam, or a truss — period — unless the manufacturer's literature allows it or an engineer signs off. Those pre stamped knockouts in an I joist web are the manufacturer's permission. A truss that got field cut needs a registered design professional. That's an easy exam point.

Floor openings, like a stairwell. If the header joist span is four feet or less, a single header the same size as the joists is fine, with single trimmers if the header lands within three feet of the trimmer bearing. Once the header span goes over four feet, double the header and double the trimmers. Over six feet, hang it on approved joist hangers. Four feet, double. Six feet, hangers.
Double joists under a parallel bearing partition that get spread apart for piping? Block between them, full depth, two inch nominal lumber, at no more than four feet on center.

Cantilevers. The twenty fifteen code says a prescriptive floor cantilever can't exceed the nominal depth of the joist — a two by ten hangs out about ten inches — beyond that you're into the cantilever tables. Here's the trap: the L over four rule, cantilever equals a quarter of the back span — that's a deck rule from the twenty twenty one I R C. It is not in the tested code. If the question says per the code, the answer is the depth rule and the tables.

Up to the walls. Stud sizes: a two by four bearing wall carrying just a roof and ceiling can go twenty four inches on center up to ten feet tall. Add one floor above, and two by fours drop to sixteen inches on center. Two floors plus a roof? Two by fours are out — you need two by sixes at sixteen. Nonbearing two by fours can run twenty four on center up to fourteen feet. Utility grade studs are the cheap seats: sixteen on center max, roof and ceiling only, eight feet max in exterior walls.

Top plates: doubled, overlapped at corners and intersections, with end joints offset at least twenty four inches. There's a single top plate exception, and it has its own hardware: a three by six inch, twenty gauge galvanized splice plate with six eight penny nails on each side. Remember twenty gauge for that one, because there's a different plate coming in a second.

Stud notching and boring — four percentages, and the exam will absolutely try to cross wire them. Notching: twenty five percent of the stud width in a bearing or exterior wall, forty percent in a nonbearing partition. Boring: forty percent in a single bearing stud, sixty percent in a nonbearing stud — or in a bearing stud if you double the studs, and you can only bore two successive doubled studs that way. Every bored hole stays five eighths of an inch from the edge of the stud, and never in the same cross section as a notch. So: notch twenty five and forty. Bore forty and sixty. The forty percent shows up on both lists — notching nonbearing, boring bearing. That's the wire they want you to cross.

Now the top plate repair. When somebody cuts or notches more than fifty percent of a bearing wall top plate — usually the plumber running a vent — the fix is a galvanized metal tie, sixteen gauge, an inch and a half wide, nailed with eight ten penny nails on each side, extending at least six inches past the opening. Sixteen gauge repair tie versus twenty gauge single plate splice. Two different plates, two different rules.

Headers over doors and windows come out of the header tables — sized by the header's lumber, the snow load, and the building width — and the same table tells you how many jack studs go under each end. Jack studs, also called trimmers, are cut to header height and carry the load. King studs run full height beside them.

Wall bracing basics. Every exterior wall line is a braced wall line, and along it, a braced wall panel has to begin within ten feet of each end of the line, with no more than twenty feet between adjacent panels. Know your method letters: L I B is a one by four let in brace. W S P is wood structural panel, minimum three eighths inch. G B is gypsum board. C S dash W S P is continuous sheathing. And in Michigan, wind governs bracing, not earthquakes — we're seismic design category A or B.

Up to the roof. The ridge board is at least one inch nominal thick, and at least as deep as the cut end of the rafter. Valley and hip rafters are beefier: two inch nominal minimum, same depth rule. And when the roof pitch drops below three in twelve, a ridge board isn't enough — the ridge, hips, and valleys have to be designed as beams.

Here is the tie question, and it is almost guaranteed to show up. Rafter ties versus collar ties. Rafter ties — usually your ceiling joists — sit down low, at the plate, and they resist the outward thrust that wants to push your walls apart. Minimum two by four when installed as dedicated ties. Collar ties sit up high, in the upper third of the attic, minimum one by four, no more than four feet on center, and they resist wind uplift at the ridge. Low ties stop spreading. High ties stop uplift. If ceiling joists run perpendicular to the rafters or aren't connected at the plate, you add rafter ties or you engineer a ridge beam.

A few more roof numbers. Ceiling joists lap at least three inches over bearing partitions, or butt and get toenailed. Purlins that shorten rafter spans must be at least the size of the rafters they support, braced down to bearing walls with two by fours at forty five degrees or steeper, braces four feet on center max, and no brace longer than eight feet unbraced. Rafter notching follows the exact same fractions as joists — one sixth, one fourth at ends, one third for holes.

Fastening schedule — table R six oh two point three. The greatest hits: joist to sill or girder, three eight penny toenails. Ceiling joist to plate, same — three eight penny toenails. Top plate to top plate, sixteen penny commons at sixteen inches on center. Double top plate splice, eight sixteen penny nails each side of the joint. Stud to plate, two sixteen penny end nails. Collar tie to rafter, three ten penny face nails. Band joist to joist, three sixteen penny end nails. Built up girders, twenty penny nails at thirty two inches on center top and bottom, staggered, with two more at every end and splice. And structural sheathing: six inches on center at the panel edges, twelve in the field.

Stairs. This is Michigan's signature amendment, so lock it down. Minimum tread depth: nine inches. Maximum riser height: eight and a quarter inches. The I R C says ten inch treads and seven and three quarter risers — in Michigan those are the trap answers. And notice the direction of the rule: nine is a minimum and eight and a quarter is a maximum, so a stair built to the stricter national numbers still passes here. Risers and treads can't vary more than three eighths of an inch within a flight. Winders: ten inches of tread at the walk line twelve inches from the narrow side, six inches minimum anywhere. Headroom: six feet eight inches. Width: thirty six inches clear, thirty one and a half with one handrail, twenty seven with two. Handrails kick in at four or more risers, set thirty four to thirty eight inches above the nosings, and a round rail grips at an inch and a quarter to two inches. Guards: required when the walking surface is more than thirty inches up, at least thirty six inches high, no opening that passes a four inch sphere, built to take a two hundred pound load.

Decks. The ledger is a minimum two by eight, pressure treated, number two grade, bolted or lag screwed with half inch hot dipped galvanized or stainless fasteners — never electroplated — spaced per the table based on joist span, staggered in two rows, and flashed where it meets the house. Where hold downs provide the lateral connection, it's two devices minimum, fifteen hundred pounds each. Deck footings go to Michigan frost depth — forty two inches. And one more trap: the deck post height table — four by four to eight feet, six by six to fourteen feet — is not in the tested code. That's the twenty twenty one I R C.

Rapid fire recap. Bearing: one and a half wood, three masonry. Bridging: only past two by twelve, eight foot intervals. Joist notch one sixth, end notch one fourth, hole one third, two inch clearances, no middle third notches. Opening headers: double past four feet, hangers past six. Stud notch twenty five bearing, forty nonbearing. Stud bore forty bearing, sixty nonbearing or doubled. Five eighths edge distance. Plate cut past fifty percent: sixteen gauge tie, inch and a half wide, eight ten penny each side, six past the cut. Plate joints offset twenty four. Two by four studs: twenty four on center roof only, sixteen with a floor above, two by six for two floors. Ridge board one inch, hips and valleys two inch, beam below three twelve. Collar ties upper third, one by four, four feet. Ceiling joist lap three inches. Purlin braces two by four, forty five degrees, four feet, eight feet max. Top plates sixteen penny at sixteen. Sheathing six and twelve. Stairs: nine inch tread, eight and a quarter riser, three eighths variation, six eight headroom, thirty six wide, handrail at four risers, thirty four to thirty eight. Guards: thirty inches triggers, thirty six high, four inch sphere, two hundred pounds. Deck: two by eight treated ledger, half inch galvanized bolts, fifteen hundred pound hold downs, forty two inch footings.
That's the chapter. Sixteen questions live in those numbers. Run this again tomorrow, and they're yours.
